      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Attention</span> <span class="qt1">Deficit</span> <span class="qt6">Hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">Disorder</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>

      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span></content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">attention</span> <span class="qt1">deficit</span> <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">disorder (</span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>)? <p><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> is a neurodevelopmental <span class="qt3">disorder</span>. It is usually first diagnosed in childhood and often lasts into adulthood. But some people don't get diagnosed with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> until they are adults. <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> involves:</p><ul><li>Having trouble paying <span class="qt0">attention</span> (inattention)</li><li>Having trouble controlling impulsive behaviors (impulsivity)</li><li>Being overly active (<span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span>)</li></ul>What are the types of <span class="qt0">attention</span> <span class="qt1">deficit</span> <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">disorder (</span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>)? <p>There are three types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>:</p><ul><li>Mostly Inattentive <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>. People with this type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> have trouble paying <span class="qt0">attention</span> and are easily distracted. It's hard for them to organize or finish tasks. They may have trouble following instructions or conversations.
</li><li>Mostly Hyperactive-Impulsive <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>. People with this type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> have symptoms of both <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> and impulsivity:
  <ul><li>With <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span>, people feel a need to always be moving. They have trouble sitting still and may fidget and/or talk too much.</li><li>With impulsivity, people have trouble controlling their actions and words. They tend to act on sudden ideas or feelings without thinking about the possible results. They may interrupt others a lot or have trouble waiting their turn.</li></ul>
</li><li>Combined <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>. People with this type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> have a mix of inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms. Combined <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> is the most common type.</li></ul><p>It's normal to sometimes have trouble paying <span class="qt0">attention</span> or sitting still, especially for children. But people with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> have more severe symptoms that can sometimes cause serious problems, for example, failing grades for a child or a job loss for an adult. The symptoms are ongoing and may affect family and social life, too.</p>What causes <span class="qt0">attention</span> <span class="qt1">deficit</span> <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">disorder (</span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>)?<p>The exact cause of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> is unknown. <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> probably results from a combination of factors, such as genetics and your environment. Researchers are looking at possible environmental factors that might raise the risk of developing <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>. These factors include brain injuries, nutrition, and social environments.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">attention</span> <span class="qt1">deficit</span> <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">disorder (</span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>)?<p>The symptoms of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> depend on the type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> a person has:</p><p>People with symptoms of <span class="qt0">attention</span> problems may often:</p><ul><li>Miss details or make careless mistakes in schoolwork, at work, or in other activities</li><li>Have trouble staying focused on play activities or work tasks</li><li>Not seem to listen when spoken to directly</li><li>Find it hard to follow instructions or finish tasks, or may start but get easily sidetracked</li><li>Have trouble being organized, keeping belongings in order, and managing time</li><li>Avoid doing tasks that require long periods of mental effort</li><li>Lose important items, such as books, wallets, keys, eyeglasses, and cellphones</li><li>Forget about doing daily activities</li></ul><p>People with symptoms of <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span>-impulsivity may often:</p><ul><li>Fidget and squirm while seated </li><li>Get up when staying seated is expected, such as at school or work</li><li>Run around or climb when it's not appropriate (children) or feel restless (teens and adults)</li><li>Have trouble doing quiet activities</li><li>Be constantly moving or "on the go"</li><li>Talk much more than is normal</li><li>Blurt out answers before questions are completed</li><li>Have trouble waiting for their turn</li><li>Interrupt others, for example, during conversations or games</li></ul><p>People with combined <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> show a mix of inattention and <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span>-impulsivity symptoms.</p>How is <span class="qt0">attention</span> <span class="qt1">deficit</span> <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">disorder (</span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>) diagnosed?<p>There is no single test to diagnose <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>. One step of the process for diagnosing <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>  involves having a physical exam, including vision tests, hearing tests (for children and adults), and other tests to rule out other problems with symptoms like <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>. Other problems with similar symptoms include anxiety, depression, sleep problems, and certain types of learning disabilities.</p><p>The process also involves a thorough medical history and family history.  And it usually includes using standardized <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> symptom checklists, questionnaires, and/or interview questions. These tools have rating scales (scoring systems) that help the provider see if a person's symptoms and history fit a diagnosis of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>.</p><p>To make a diagnosis of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>, the provider needs to have found all of these things:</p><ul><li>Several symptoms of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> that began before age 12.</li><li>Several symptoms of inattention and/or <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span>-impulsivity that have lasted for at least 6 months and cause serious problems:</li><ul><li>For children up to age 16, there must be at least 6 ongoing symptoms.</li><li>For people 17 and older, there must be at least 5 ongoing symptoms.</li><li>Symptoms that happen in 2 or more settings, for example, at home and at work or school.</li><li>Symptoms that clearly get in the way of functioning well at school, work, and/or in social situations.</li><li>Symptoms aren't caused by another mental health <span class="qt3">disorder</span>.</li></ul></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">attention</span> <span class="qt1">deficit</span> <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">disorder (</span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>)?<p>Although there is no cure for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>, treatments may help reduce symptoms and improve functioning. <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span> is commonly treated with:</p><ul><li>Medicines.</li><li>Psychotherapy (talk therapy), including behavior therapy.</li><li>Education or training for parents to give them the skills and strategies to help their child. This is especially important for younger children.</li><li>A combination of these treatments.</li></ul><p>Good treatment plans will include close monitoring, follow-ups, and making changes, if needed, along the way.</p><p>Having a healthy lifestyle, such as healthy eating and regular exercise, may also help manage symptoms.</p><p>For school-aged children, school support is important. This could include classroom-based behavioral interventions such as behavior management plans or teaching your child organizational and study skills. It may also include accommodations such as specific seating in the classroom, reduced classwork, or extended time on tests and exams.</p><p></p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health </p></content>

      <content name="title">Congenital Heart Defects</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Heart Defects</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Heart <span class="qt4">Diseases</span>, Congenital</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Heart Murmur</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are congenital heart defects?<p>Congenital heart defects (CHDs) are problems with the structure of the heart. "Congenital" means that that the problems are present at birth. These defects happen when a fetus's heart doesn't develop normally during pregnancy. Congenital heart defects are the most common type of birth defect.</p><p>Congenital heart defects can change the way the heart pumps blood. They may make blood flow too slowly, go the wrong way, or block it completely.</p><p>There are many types of congenital heart defects. They can happen in one or more parts of the heart. The most common types are:</p><ul><li>Septal defects ("hole in the heart") - openings in the wall between the left and right sides of the heart</li><li>Heart valve defects - problems with the valves that control the flow of blood through the heart</li><li>Defects in the large blood vessels that carry blood in and out of the heart</li></ul><p>Congenital heart defects can range from very mild problems that never need treatment to life-threatening problems at birth. The most serious congenital heart defects are called critical congenital heart <span class="qt4">disease</span>. Babies with these defects usually need surgery in the first year of life. But the symptoms of milder heart defects may not show up until childhood or adulthood.</p>What causes congenital heart defects?<p>Researchers often don't know what causes congenital heart defects. They do know that changes in a baby's genes sometimes cause a heart defect. The changed genes may come from the parents, or the changes may happen during pregnancy.</p>Who is more likely to have a baby with a congenital heart defect?<p>Several things may increase the chance that your baby has a congenital heart defect, such as:</p><ul><li>Your health before and during pregnancy, including:
	<ul><li>Having diabetes before pregnancy or developing it in the first 3 months of pregnancy (diabetes that develops later in pregnancy isn't a major risk for heart defects). Carefully controlling your blood glucose, also called blood sugar, before and during pregnancy can lower your baby's risk of congenital heart defects.</li><li>Having phenylketonuria (PKU), a rare inherited <span class="qt3">disorder</span> that affects how the body uses a protein in foods. If you have PKU, eating a low-protein diet before getting pregnant can lower your baby's risk of having a congenital heart defect.</li><li>Having rubella (German measles) during pregnancy.</li></ul></li><li>Your contact with certain substances during pregnancy, including:
	<ul><li>Smoking or secondhand smoke (breathing smoke from another smoker).</li><li>Certain medicines, such as angiotensin-converting (ACE) inhibitors for high blood pressure and retinoic acids for acne. If you're pregnant or plan to get pregnant, talk with your health care provider about all the medicines you take.</li></ul></li><li>Your family history and genetics. In most cases, congenital heart defects don't run in families. But your chance of having a baby with a congenital heart defect does go up if you or the other parent has a congenital heart defect, or if you already have a child with a congenital heart defect.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of congenital heart defects?<p>Congenital heart defects don't cause pain. The signs and symptoms are different, depending on the type and number of defects and how serious they are.</p><p>Common signs and symptoms of congenital heart defects include:</p><ul><li>Cyanosis - a bluish color to the skin, lips, and fingernails. It happens when there isn't enough oxygen in the blood.</li><li>Fatigue - your baby may be unusually sleepy and may become very tired during feedings.</li><li>Poor blood flow.</li><li>Fast or difficult breathing.</li><li>Heart murmur - an unusual sound between heartbeats.</li></ul>What other problems do congenital heart defects cause?<p>Congenital heart defects don't always cause other problems. If they do, which problems you have would depend on the type and number of defects and how serious the defects are.</p><p>Children with congenital heart defects are more likely to:</p><ul><li>Be smaller than other children</li><li>Have problems or delays in mental, and emotional growth, and behavior, such as:
	<ul><li>Speech and language problems</li><li><span class="qt0">Attention</span> <span class="qt1">deficit</span> <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">disorder (</span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>)</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>People with congenital heart defects may develop other health conditions, including:</p><ul><li>Endocarditis - an infection of lining of the heart and valves</li><li>Arrhythmia - a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat</li><li>Heart failure - when your heart can't pump enough blood to the body</li><li>Pulmonary hypertension - high blood pressure in your lungs</li><li>Kidney and liver <span class="qt4">disease</span></li></ul>How are congenital heart defects diagnosed?<ul><li>Before a baby is born, your provider may use ultrasound pictures of the fetus's heart to look for heart defects. This is called a fetal echocardiogram. It's done between weeks 18 and 22 of pregnancy.</li><li>During the first few days after birth, all newborns are checked for congenital heart defects. A pulse oximeter is clipped to your baby's hands or feet to measure blood oxygen. If it shows low levels of blood oxygen, more tests will be needed to find out if your baby has a heart defect.</li><li>To diagnose congenital heart defects in babies, children, and adults, a provider may use many tools, including:
	<ul><li>A physical exam.</li><li>Certain heart tests to see how the heart is working.</li><li>Genetic testing to see if certain gene problems caused the defect.</li></ul></li></ul>What are the treatments for congenital heart defects?<p>Treatment depends on the type of congenital heart defect and how serious it is. Possible treatments include:</p><ul><li>Cardiac catheterization to repair simple defects, such as a small hole in the inside wall of the heart. A catheterization uses a thin tube guided through a vein and into the heart.</li><li>Heart surgery may be needed to:
	<ul><li>Repair defects in the heart and blood vessels.</li><li>Repair or replace a heart valve.</li><li>Place a device in the chest to help the heart pump blood.</li><li>Do a heart transplant</li></ul>
</li><li>Medicine is often used if your baby has a specific type of congenital heart defect called patent ductus arteriosus.</li></ul><p>All children and adults who have congenital heart defects need regular follow-up care from a cardiologist (a doctor who specializes in heart <span class="qt4">diseases</span>) throughout their life, even if their defect was repaired.</p><p>Some people may need several heart surgeries or catheterizations over the years. They may also need to take medicines to help their hearts work as well as possible.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Tourette Syndrome</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>If you have Tourette syndrome, you make unusual movements or sounds, called tics. You have little or no control over them. Common tics are throat-clearing and blinking. You may repeat words, spin, or, rarely, blurt out swear words. </p><p>Tourette syndrome is a <span class="qt3">disorder</span> of the nervous system. It often occurs with other problems, such as:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Attention</span> <span class="qt1">deficit</span> <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">disorder  (</span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>)</li><li>Obsessive-compulsive <span class="qt3">disorder</span>  (OCD)</li><li>Anxiety</li><li>Depression</li></ul><p>The cause of Tourette syndrome is unknown. It is more common in boys than girls. The tics usually start in childhood and may be worst in the early teens.  Many people eventually outgrow them. </p><p>No treatment is needed unless the tics interfere with everyday life. Excitement or worry can make tics worse. Calm, focused activities may make them better. Medicines and talk therapy may also help.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Neurological <span class="qt3">Disorders</span> and Stroke</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/teendepression.html">
      <content name="title">Teen Depression</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Depression, Teen</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is depression in teens?<p>Depression in teens (ages 13-17) is a serious medical <span class="qt4">illness</span>. It's more than just a feeling of being sad or "blue" for a few days. It is an intense feeling of sadness, hopelessness, and anger or frustration that lasts much longer. These feelings make it hard for you to function normally and do your usual activities. You may also have trouble focusing and have no motivation or energy. Depression can make you feel like it is hard to enjoy life or even get through the day.</p>What causes depression in teens?<p>Many factors may play a role in depression, including:</p><ul><li>Genetics. Depression can run in families.</li><li>Brain biology and chemistry.</li><li>Hormones. Hormone changes can contribute to depression.</li><li>Stressful childhood events such as trauma, the death of a loved one, bullying, and abuse.</li></ul>Which teens are at risk of depression?<p>Depression can happen at any age, but often begins in the teens or early adulthood. Certain teens are at higher risk of depression, such as those who:</p><ul><li>Have other mental health conditions, such as anxiety, eating <span class="qt3">disorders</span>, and substance use</li><li>Have other <span class="qt4">diseases</span>, such as diabetes, cancer, and heart <span class="qt4">disease</span></li><li>Have family members with <span class="qt4">mental illness</span></li><li>Have a dysfunctional family/family conflict</li><li>Have problems with friends or other kids at school</li><li>Have learning disabilities or <span class="qt0">attention</span> <span class="qt1">deficit</span> <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">disorder (</span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>)</li><li>Have had trauma in childhood</li><li>Have low self-esteem, a pessimistic outlook, or poor coping skills</li></ul>What are the symptoms of depression in teens?<p>If you have depression, you have one or more of these symptoms most of the time:</p><ul><li>Sadness</li><li>Feeling of emptiness</li><li>Hopelessness</li><li>Being angry, irritable, or frustrated, even at minor things</li></ul><p>You also may also have other symptoms, such as:</p><ul><li>No longer caring about things you used to enjoy</li><li>Changes in weight, such as losing weight when you are not dieting or gaining weight from eating too much</li><li>Changes in sleep, such as having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, or sleeping much more than usual</li><li>Feeling restless or having trouble sitting still</li><li>Feeling very tired or not having energy</li><li>Feeling worthless or very guilty</li><li>Having trouble concentrating, remembering information, or making decisions</li><li>Thinking about dying or suicide</li></ul>How is depression in teens diagnosed?<p>If you think you might be depressed, tell someone that you trust, such as your:</p><ul><li>Parents or guardian</li><li>Teacher or counselor</li><li>Doctor</li></ul><p>The next step is to see your doctor for a checkup. Your doctor can first make sure that you do not have another health problem that is causing your depression. To do this, you may have a physical exam and lab tests.</p><p>If you don't have another health problem, you will get a psychological evaluation. Your doctor may do it, or you may be referred to a mental health professional to get one. You may be asked about things such as:</p><ul><li>Your thoughts and feelings</li><li>How you are doing at school</li><li>Any changes in your eating, sleeping, or energy level</li><li>Whether you are suicidal</li><li>Whether you use alcohol or drugs</li></ul>How is depression in teens treated?<p>Effective treatments for depression in teens include talk therapy, or a combination of talk therapy and medicines:</p><p>Talk therapy</p><p>Talk therapy, also called psychotherapy or counseling, can help you understand and manage your moods and feelings. It involves going to see a therapist, such as a psychiatrist, a psychologist, a social worker, or counselor. You can talk out your emotions to someone who understands and supports you. You can also learn how to stop thinking negatively and start to look at the positives in life. This will help you build confidence and feel better about yourself.</p><p>There are many different types of talk therapy. Certain types have been shown to help teens deal with depression, including:</p><ul><li>Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which helps you to identify and change negative and unhelpful thoughts. It also helps you build coping skills and change behavioral patterns.</li><li>Interpersonal therapy (IPT), which focuses on improving your relationships. It helps you understand and work through troubled relationships that may contribute to your depression. IPT may help you change behaviors that are causing problems.  You also explore major issues that may add to your depression, such as grief or life changes.</li></ul><p>Medicines</p><p>In some cases, your doctor will suggest medicines along with talk therapy. There are a few antidepressants that have been widely studied and proven to help teens. If you are taking medicine for depression, it is important to see your doctor regularly.</p><p>It is also important to know that it will take some time for you to get relief from antidepressants:</p><ul><li>It can take 3 to 4 weeks until an antidepressant takes effect</li><li>You may have to try more than one antidepressant to find one that works for you</li><li>It can also take some time to find the right dose of an antidepressant</li></ul><p>In some cases, teenagers may have an increase in suicidal thoughts or behavior when taking antidepressants. This risk is higher in the first few weeks after starting the medicine and when the dose is changed. Make sure to tell your parents or guardian if you start feeling worse or have thoughts of hurting yourself.</p><p>You should not stop taking the antidepressants on your own. You need to work with your doctor to slowly and safely decrease the dose before you stop.</p><p>Programs for severe depression</p><p>Some teens who have severe depression or are at risk of hurting themselves may need more intensive treatment. They may go into a psychiatric hospital or do a day program. Both offer counseling, group discussions, and activities with mental health professionals and other patients. Day programs may be full-day or half-day, and they often last for several weeks.</p></content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is a learning disability?<p>Learning disabilities are conditions that affect the ability to learn. They can cause problems with:</p><ul><li>Understanding what people are saying</li><li>Speaking</li><li>Reading</li><li>Writing</li><li>Doing math</li><li>Paying <span class="qt0">attention</span></li></ul><p>Often, children have more than one kind of learning disability. They may also have another condition, such as <span class="qt0">attention</span> <span class="qt1">deficit</span> <span class="qt6">hyperactivity</span> <span class="qt3">disorder (</span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>).  This can make learning even more of a challenge. The sooner a learning disability is identified and addressed, the better a child is likely to perform in school.</p>What causes learning disabilities?<p>Learning disabilities don't have anything to do with how smart your child is. They are caused by differences in the brain, and they affect the way the brain takes in and uses information. These differences are usually present at birth. But there are certain factors that can play a role in the development of a learning disability, including:</p><ul><li>Genetics</li><li>Environmental exposures, such as lead</li><li>Using substances while pregnant</li></ul>How are learning disabilities diagnosed?<p>The earlier you can find and treat a learning disability, the better. Unfortunately, learning disabilities are usually not found until a child is in school. If you notice that your child is struggling, talk to your child's teacher or health care provider about having your child evaluated for a learning disability. The evaluation may include:</p><ul><li>Doing a physical exam to check for a medical problem that might make learning more difficult.</li><li>Asking about your family history.</li><li>Test your child's intellectual and school performance.</li></ul>What are the treatments for learning disabilities?<p>The most common treatment for learning disabilities is special education. A teacher or other learning specialist can help your child learn skills by building on their strengths and finding ways to make up for their weaknesses. They may suggest ways you can help your child when they do homework. Instructors may try special teaching methods, make changes to the classroom, or use technologies that can assist your child's learning needs. Some children also get help from tutors or speech or language therapists.</p><p>A child with a learning disability may struggle with low self-esteem, frustration, and other problems. Mental health professionals can help your child understand these feelings, develop coping tools, and build healthy relationships.</p><p>If your child has another condition, such as <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt6">ADHD</span></span></span></span>, they will need treatment for that condition as well.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development</p></content>
